utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, while we're waiting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wanted to get an answer to my question. Why did I get the witness statement, statement of the witness who was planned for tomorrow only yesterday? As far as I know, according to all the plans here, witness statements are given a month in advance. It is only in my case that the Rules are violated all the time, even the decisions that you yourselves make. As for the witness Sandra Mitchell, it was really drastic, and the registrar of the court can confirm to you that I got this only yesterday. Secondly, I cautioned you yesterday that on the 17th of April, when you limited my time for cross-examination to one hour, you said that the other side should give introductory remarks for five minutes. In the meantime, that changed. The other side practically has unlimited time and you've shortened my time to 45 minutes. Lest I be misunderstood --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've dealt with all these matters. Let me deal with your first point, about the witness. There seems to be some problem with the transcript. Are we going to get the transcript now? The accused has raised two points, not for the first time. The first point that he raises is that he is limited to 45 minutes whereas the Prosecution are taking longer than the five minutes which was allotted to them. That's a point which we have in mind. However, the five minutes was not a mandatory time. It's necessary sometimes for the witnesses' evidence to be summarised in rather longer form. It's the only opportunity for that evidence to be heard, some of it dealing with horrifying events. The reason that we limit your time, as I have pointed out often enough, is that you waste it, and the Court has to protect itself against being abused by time wasting. I turn to your next point. There is a power within the Court to abridge the time allowed for any witness statements, and in the case of the witness you mention, Sandra Mitchell, her evidence, we are told, was served on you on the 27th of June. That was short. However, we have ensured that that witness will not give evidence until tomorrow, so you will have adequate time to prepare for it. The only point of the Rule is that you should have adequate time to prepare before a witness gives evidence, and that we keep in mind continually when we review these decisions. Yes. We'll have the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. This is not -- Mr. Milosevic, we must get on. Time is short. We cannot spend time arguing -- listening to you arguing points which have been decided. We will hear you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was said was inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will hear you in due course when we come to deal with administrative matters. But during the time for the hearing of witnesses, we need to be hearing the witnesses. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution calls Mustafa Draga. And while the witness is being brought into the courtroom, I will use the time, if I may, to assist the Court. If you'll turn to the Kosovo atlas 2, page 5. On page 5, the -- between numbers 30 and 40, you will see the quadrangle on the right-hand side of the page. The village is Lecina, and that would be about the left part of that right quadrant, if I can call it that, between 30 and 40, just about an inch or so north of Izbica. That's the area we're going to be talking about with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Draga, I understand, sir, that you are 64 years old and you are a Kosovo Albanian Muslim from the village of Lecina in Srbica, Skenderaj municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And I understand, sir, that you are married and you have ten children; eight sons and two daughters?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Is it true, sir, that in March of 1999, four of those sons and one of your daughters still lived at home with you and your wife?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you give statements to investigators of the ICTY on the 11th and 13th of November of 1999?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And about a month ago, did you have a chance to read those statements over again or have them read to you in your own language and then appear before a presiding officer of this Tribunal and say that -- make a solemn declaration that those statements are true to the best of your knowledge, information, and belief? Did you do that on the 10th of June -- I'm sorry, on the 8th of March, 2002?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to at this time tender the 92 bis statements of this witness and have those marked as an exhibit. And while that's being done, I propose to use the time by reading a very brief summary of what is contained in those statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Within the five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: It's a two-page summary, so I'll either have to read fast or skim, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me. Prosecution Exhibit 237 and 237A for the redacted version.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honours, you've heard that in March of 1999, the witness was an occupant or resident of Lecina, but in July of 1998, he talks about, in his statement, the Serb police entering the area around his village and establishing checkpoints. He indicates that the villages in his area were occasionally shelled and some people were killed. The villages of Padaliste and Citak were partly burned in 1998. The witness and his wife left Lecina and stayed in Mitrovica for three months, while his sons and daughters went on to Montenegro. You will find in his statement that they all returned to Lecina in October of 1998 when the OSCE arrived. In his statement, he describes that on the 25th of March of 1999, Lecina and other villages in the area were shelled from the direction of Bjelica and Padaliste. That shelling continued the following day and he could see the Serb forces getting closer and could observe burning houses. As a result, he and his family were one of the last families to leave for Izbica, which apparently was considered to be a safer place. They left on the 26th of March. They then stayed in a field, of which you've heard evidence from other witnesses, outside Izbica, together with his family; and he estimates that there were several thousand other refugees in this large field. On the 27th of March, he observed that villages around Izbica were burning, and he mentions the various villages of Broje, Vojnik, Bllozina, Lower Klina, Jashanice and Ozrim. He indicates that the younger men among the refugees went into hiding in the woods. On the morning of the 28th of March, 1999, he saw Serb forces advancing towards Izbica and surrounding the village. He estimates that there were about 300 soldiers or even more. He describes their uniforms and the fact that they had Milicija on their uniform sleeves, and he gives a description in his statement of what they were wearing. When those forces arrived, they separated the men from the women, leaving the boys under the age of 13 with their mothers. The troops demanded money from the crowd and the witness saw many people handing over money. Because he didn't have any money, he was hit with a rifle butt by one of the soldiers. They were also verbally harassed. He then describes how one of the police officers lined up the men, divided them into two groups and ordered them to walk in an easterly and westerly direction respectively, towards the woods. He describes the police officer in charge and that there were about 70 men in his group. In his statement, he names 16 of them that he knew from the Lecina area. After walking about 500 metres, the men were ordered to stop and turn around. He saw approximately 30 police officers close to them. He then tells you that the police commenced shooting immediately upon the men turning around. The witness fell to the ground when the shooting started, and another man whom he names, also by the name of Draga, fell over top of him. He was wounded, that is, the man who fell on him. Bullets were striking all around the witness and he heard cries of pain from those who were hit. The witness was not struck by any bullets and remained uninjured but he lay still, under the other man who had fallen on top of him, until the shooting stopped. He describes that what sounded like continuous automatic fire lasted for one or two minutes. He continued to remain quiet for about 20 to 30 minutes, during which time he heard gunfire from some distance. And then he observed the police set fire to the houses in Izbica. When he thought it was safe, he crawled into the nearby woods where he found some other survivors. They stayed in the woods for the next two days. He then describes in his statement the aftermath. On Tuesday, the 30th of March, they went to other villages. They buried the dead. They found the bodies of four people killed on the tractors in the field, among them a paralysed woman, Zoja Osmana, who was burned on a trailer. You will recall some months ago hearing from some of the women who talked about this incident as well. The commander, a KLA commander who was present on the 30th and 31st, made a detailed list of the bodies, and the witness also heard that other bodies were subsequently buried in the same place but he didn't see that. He then describes how he stayed in the woods with hundreds of others for about six weeks, until after NATO arrived in Kosovo, and tells you eventually that he returned to Izbica for three to four days and then back to Lecina where he found his house destroyed by fire, his cows missing, his car burnt, and his tractor damaged. That is a very brief summary of these events. Needless to say, I cannot do justice to his statement in five minutes, but that is an overview. Those are all the questions I have of the witness as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Draga, when they separated you, you had been in a group with a number of citizens from many villages around Izbica. Did I understand your statement correctly?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes. They divided us and lined us up in two and kept us there and insulted us, and they asked us money and then we were struck. And then they divided us in two groups, and one they took to the west and one to the east. I was in the eastern group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And -- and how many citizens were there in that field, in that meadow where you say that you were surrounded, insulted, et cetera? How many citizens were there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: On the 27th, there were 15 or 16.000. And then some went to Tushile and we were 5 or 6.000 left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There were 15, 16.000 persons on that day when you were being executed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: No. When we were executed, we were about 5 or 6.000 of us. On the 27th, many left and the majority went to the village of Tushile.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So when they executed you, there were 5 or 6.000. You say that they separated the men and they took them to be executed. Does that mean that all the rest were women and children?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: The remainder were women and children, and they sent them off in the directions of Turiqevc and Vojnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Out of the 5 or 6.000 of you, only about 150 of you were men, those that they had singled out, as you had put it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes. There were more, but those who were killed were 144.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. How far away were you when they executed you? How far away were you from this group of 5.000 persons? You said that you went a few hundred -- a few hundred metres away from them, towards the woods.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Excuse me: First they took away the women, the children, and then they divided us into two groups and sent one group to the east and one to the west. The women were -- had taken away about 5 or 600 metres away from us when we were executed. They were walking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that means that they first took the women and children, and then there was no one there in the field when they executed you; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the meaning of that question? It seems absolutely pointless comment, Mr. Milosevic. Of course there were people there when they were -- the executions took place. Are you challenging that the executions took place? Are you challenging the witness's evidence about that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, of course, Mr. May. Before him you had here Milazim Thaci who explained that he had also been executed. And he was also saved by God, just like Mr. Draga, who was executed by a heavy machine-gun from an eight-metre distance. And the exhibit, the photograph with a shirt with holes in it is one that you admitted. So of course I'm challenging it. I'm challenging this too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you suggesting the witness is not telling the truth about this? Is that the suggestion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but the Court is striving to find the truth, and the accused should have been among us and see how people were killed and massacred and how the villages were burned. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you survived because God saved you; right? They missed you. They missed you, judging by your statement, at a distance of only a few metres. They -- they tried to execute you with a heavy machine-gun at close range; right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I was saved by God to come here and testify to the truth, because only God saved me from the Serbian police. Because they shot me. They massacred people, they burned, they slaughtered people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Draga. In your statement, you describe the following: That they separated you out of this big group of people and took you a few hundred metres away, towards the woods. And now you say that previously, this group of people out of which you were singled out was taken somewhere and then you were taken towards the woods. What is correct; the first or the second?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, because you're trying to provoke me. But first they separated the women and sent them to Turiqevc. Then they lined up the men in the road and they insulted us, and then they said, "What relationship do you have to Thaci?" And then they divided us into two groups and they sent one group to the west and one to the east. I was in the eastern group and Milazim was in the western group. These are just your provocations. And that's what I said in my statement, and these things are true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's be very precise about this. In the statement, you did not mention that, first of all, they took all these people away. And now you claim that they took all these people away somewhere before they executed you, and you say that they took them 5 or 600 metres away. That means that they had to see that, they had to see when you were being executed, these 5 or 6.000 people. Didn't they have to see that? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- before the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, the witness should have the opportunity of dealing with it. Can he read a statement? Just a moment, Mr. Draga, we'll try to sort this out. Can he read the statement, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I do believe he is able to. Whether or not his glasses -- or whether he needs them, that's something I don't recall. But just the last suggestion by the accused, if I could invite you to turn with me to page 4 of the English version of the admitted statement, the second full paragraph specifically says: "The women and children were moved farther away from us and then told to start walking in the direction of Turiqevc." Then he talks about splitting them up into east and west. So what the accused is saying to this witness is not fair because it's right in his summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. He says: "This group go to the east. This group go to the west. The group I was in --" let us go through it. "The group I was in numbered about 70 men. We were then told to walk in the direction indicated." Then there's a description of the policemen. Then there is the names of the people who were in his group. "We walked, I would estimate, for approximately 500 metres, not more, up the hill towards the east side of the valley." Policemen shouted at them. "We turned round," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's the point, Your Honour, I was trying to make, that the witness [sic] said that he hadn't said it in his statement and it's not fair to suggest that. Perhaps we could supply a copy in the Albanian language to the witness. I'll try to be on my guard where there are unfair characterisations of his statement put to him in the questions, but I can't get them all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you must not mislead witnesses by putting to them things which are inaccurate. It's neither fair to the witness nor is it right that you should try and mislead the Court in this way. Now, let the witness have a copy of his statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to establish, Mr. May, how far away from them all these people in the group were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. No need to read it for the minute. Mr. Milosevic, you can ask that. That is a perfectly fair question. But what you mustn't do is mischaracterise what a witness has said in his statement. Now, the question, Mr. Draga, for you, is this: How far -- when the execution took place, how far away were the main group of people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were about 500 metres away - they were walking - more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you were going, as I understood now that this part of your statement was read again, you were going uphill in relation to them.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: We were going up the hill to the hill where they executed us. But these seem to me provocative questions because these are true events. These are not -- this is not false testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Draga, you must bear with us. The accused is entitled to ask some questions to establish the truth and to clarify events. So if you would just bear with him and just deal with the questions. If the questions are unfair, as you've seen, he'll be stopped.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. I'm sorry, on your account too, because we had considerable --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since you were uphill compared to that group and the group was 500 away from you, does that mean that this group of people were eyewitnesses to that execution and that you were being executed at a distance of 500 metres, in plain sight of this large group of people, 5 or 6.000 people?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: These people were walking towards Turiqevc and Klina. I don't know whether they were able to see it or not. They were being escorted as they walked. They were walking away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can understand that, but I assume that at a distance of 500 metres, shooting is heard loud and clear. So when there is shooting, do you suppose that this is something that can attract one's attention and that if you are standing on a hill while being executed, people at the foot of the hill can see it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's already answered that. He said he doesn't know whether the people could have heard or seen or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. The policemen were not more than four or five metres from us, not 500 metres. They were all on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Draga. This whole issue is clear to me. Could you tell me now, if you know, specifically in your area, that from the 24th of March until the 29th of March, important battles were waged between our army and the police on the one hand and the KLA on the other?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: As far as I know, the KLA didn't fight at all because it was unable to. It didn't have weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you are saying the KLA had no weapons and that's why they didn't fight at all?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Well, it had weapons. It had some terrible guns. It didn't have guns and tanks and heavy equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know that in your area there were about two and a half thousand members of the KLA and all of them were armed? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I don't know that there were 2.500. I didn't see very much of them because I didn't stay at home very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell me how many you did see? You didn't see two and a half thousand, but how many did you see?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I saw a dozen. I didn't take much interest in these matters at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, then, later, as far as I understood also from the statement of Milazim Thaci and from other events, you were saying that a funeral had been organised. And we have already established that this funeral was organised by the KLA. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: There were more civilians. There weren't many KLA members at the funeral. It was Sadik Xhemajli who was the first to organise it, and he organised the lists of names. There were very few members of the KLA present that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this Sadik Xhemajli, a commander of the KLA, was he there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That presupposes that the witness knows, if it's true, that he was commander of the KLA. Was he the commander of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sadik Xhemajli wasn't commander of the KLA. It was merely he who organised the funeral that day in Izbica. I don't know whether he was a commander or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know whether he was a commander. All right. And is it correct that some young men from your own village were also members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: There were some. How many there were, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And could you tell me, were there any Serbs living in your village?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: There were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was your relationship with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: To a certain extent, it wasn't -- they weren't too bad. Average. But then later on, these relations were totally disrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said in your statement that in the summer, in July 1998, the Serb police came to your area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: 1998? Yes. The Serbian police came in 1998, and they took me to the police station and beat me several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And could you now tell me, please, where is that in your statement? I couldn't find it. Perhaps someone can assist me. This part when you say that in 1998, too, you were taken to the police and beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes. They took us in 1998, because in 1999, we fled as far as we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say in the beginning of your statement, last paragraph, in the summer of 1998, in July, the Serbian police came to the area and established checkpoints. Things became tense, and so on and so forth. Shelling of the village. Many people left the area for their own safety. Some of them went to Montenegro, others took Kosovska Mitrovica. We left our home and we were away for almost three months. We went to Kosovska Mitrovica and we stayed there while our sons and our daughter went to Montenegro. You don't mention anywhere that you were taken to the police station in 1998 and beaten up. Why didn't you mention such an important thing?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I didn't mention -- this was before 1998 that they took me, not in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. When before 1998?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I don't know the date. But they took me from the yard, and they didn't even allow me to put my clothes on. And for three days in succession they kept me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it in 1997, 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... says the witness in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What time in 1997?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: It was in winter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean in end 1997 or in early 1997?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: It must have been the end of 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why were you taken to the police station?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: They took us because after 1991, we had no peace. We've never -- we've always had trouble and we've been beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So starting with 1991, you were beaten?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: You know all these things very well. I don't know why you're asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know and can you tell me, at that time in 1998, in July, when you say that the police established checkpoints, what happened before that to cause the police to come? What is it that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. happened in your area to make the police come and establish checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Nothing happened. What happened were your orders. And as the whole world can see, an innocent population and defenseless people ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you know absolutely nothing about things that happened in your area? You know nothing about killings, kidnappings, crimes committed by the KLA at that time when the police established checkpoints, or you know something at least?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I don't know anything. I was in Mitrovica. I was in the hills. I don't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, before the police established checkpoints - that means before July 1998 when you say the checkpoints were established, after which you left the village - do you know what had happened before that time, while you were still in the village?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Nothing happened. We didn't dare go to the checkpoints. In the last ten years, we've had no end of trouble. I don't know why you're asking questions, because you know yourself what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know -- or, rather, is it true that it was precisely in that period, in the month of March, the so-called 145th Brigade of the KLA was in your area? Have you heard about it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I don't know where they were stationed, so I don't know anything about a brigade with this number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Do you know anything about any brigade without a number or with a different number?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I said I wasn't interested where -- as to who they were, where they were. I wasn't interested. I was only interested in my own family, looking after my family and staying with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was perhaps the reason for the establishment of the checkpoints the presence of the KLA in your area?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I don't know. I think you would know that better than I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In your statement, you say that on the 25th of March, before the NATO bombing of Serbia, Serbs came into the village of Lecina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: When NATO bombed, they entered into Leqina. I think it was the 26th. The 25th, they set off, and the 26th, they burnt the whole neighbourhood down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say on the 25th of March. That is on the page which ends with 36. The number is long. You say the day before NATO started bombing the Serbs. Do you know that the bombing started actually on the 24th?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: According to the English translation, that's what it says. "On the 25th of March, the day after NATO commenced the bombing offensive against the Serbs." So in English, it looks like he's right on the date, if that was the date.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May. In B/C/S, it says differently, and that's why I quoted it. And if you think it's incorrect, have the B/C/S version checked again. But let me ask another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said NATO started bombing the Serbs. Did NATO bomb only the Serbs in Kosovo or they bombed all of Kosovo and all of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that's not a question for the witness. Was there any bombing in your area, any NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was nothing from NATO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, if the witness says that NATO started bombing the Serbs and I ask him a question about it, whether the NATO bombed only the Serbs or they bombed Kosovo and all of Yugoslavia, I suppose it's a legitimate question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. He's given his evidence. He can give evidence about what he saw or heard himself. As for the wider matters, they're matters which we'll have to decide.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That means that he speaks in his statement about things that he had not seen with his own eyes. And I'm sticking to his statement, and I have to make a selection from his own statement, dividing things into those that he saw with his own eyes and those he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did you get the information that Serb forces shelled the Lecina? Did you see that yourself?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I didn't say that Serbian forces did the shelling. It was Serbian military forces, not NATO, that carried out this bombardment. And the Serb -- and the NATO forces didn't bomb either the Albanians or the Serbs but simply the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you see the shelling of the Lecina village?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Whose bombardment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I mean any shelling of the village. Did you see the shelling of Lecina village? That's what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: There was no bombing. I'm not talking about the Klina e Ulta, I'm talking about our village. There were mortars and there was shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But did you see yourself what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: There was no way of seeing. We -- we saw because bullets came around our feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What bullets came around your feet?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Excuse me, what kind of bullets? The bullets that they were shooting. They were mostly mortars, but they had other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what fell around your feet were mortar shells. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: It was mortars that were fired in the hills where we were hiding, but I don't know what those provocative questions are about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to establish whether you had seen the shelling of Lecina village, and I hear from you that projectiles were falling around your feet. And then, in the next breath, you say those were mortar shells. I'm trying to establish whether it's really true, whether you're really saying that mortar shells were falling around your feet.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: These things are true, whether they were mortars or grenade throwers or machine-guns. But we were trying to get away and we couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where were you at the time? Were you in the village or up in the hills?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: On that day, on the 26th, they were shelling at 5.00, and they shelled my brother's house and shells fell in my yard too. And then I stayed in the hills of Izbica, and every day they were shelling with mortars from Broje and from Vojnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what was it that they shelled every day? Was it your village or the hills where you were hiding?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: They shelled the hills and the woods for a week on end, until we got the bodies out at Izbica, and they were shelling continually until they allowed us to fetch the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you saw bodies near Izbica. And these bodies, were they the bodies of people executed by a firing squad?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: They were the bodies of the men who were shot and executed. They were burned. Most of them had lost half their heads. It was the machine-gun fire. I don't know what kind of fire it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you've just told us that you were hiding up in the hills which were being shelled, and then later you came and saw bodies near Izbica and started gathering the corpses. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I'm talking about the day of the funeral, because I can't -- I didn't see anything more of the bodies. I was trying to save my own life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a second, Mr. Draga. You explained a moment ago, and I'm following the sequence of your explanations, and will you be so kind as to tell me whether I'm right. Your village of Lecina was shelled. Due to that shelling, as projectiles were falling around your feet, you ran away to the hills. You were hiding there. The hills were shelled, and then you reached Izbica, saw the bodies, and started picking them up. That's what you have told us a moment ago. Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: When I came out of Leqina, there were -- there was shelling, and the executions were on the 28th of March, on the day of Bajram. And these were your police. And then the police said to us, "This is Bajram. You can slaughter lambs. We're going to slaughter you."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that's what they told you, that they would slaughter you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: That's what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you write that in your statement? It's such an important thing.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: It's possible I didn't remember to write it. But that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So from these hills where you were hiding after you had fled from your village, Lecina, and from the shells that were falling, you came and you gathered bodies around Izbica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: We went to Izbica on the 26th. We got out of our houses, and the boys and the women went out earlier. I went out in the evening. On the 26th -- on the 27th, we stayed there all day. On the 28th, they came about 10.00, although I didn't have a clock, and the police came and surrounded us and divided us from the women and lined us up, insulted us, asked for money, beat us. And as I said before, they sent us towards the east and the west. And the bodies lay there from Sunday and Wednesday. And I wasn't saying that I collected the bodies from the woods or that there were bodies when I went out of Leqina that day. These seem to me to be pointless questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you just repeated your story from the beginning now, which does not correspond to what you said awhile ago concerning your flight from the village of Lecina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. He made it quite plain. If anything, it was you, Mr. Milosevic, who have been confusing the issue by your questions. His story is quite clear about where he went. Now, time is wearing on. I should think you have two or three more questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. This is a photograph of the OTP. Who made this photograph of the killed near Izbica?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please be so kind as to have this photograph shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I wonder if I might see it before it's shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means. By all means, do take a look. Is it exactly that photograph, Mr. Ryneveld?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see very well, but Liri Loshi did that, and Mr. Thaci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that photograph was taken. These are the persons who were executed, right, the persons that you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you in that group of people? Were you or were you not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which group of people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which group?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you say -- I mean, you say that there was a group of people that were executed by the Serb police, and this photograph was taken by this -- I can't remember his name right now, the name of the person you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: Liri Loshi made the photograph. I said they executed us in two groups, one in the west, one in the east. I was in the east. And I carried bodies with my sons and with the tractor, where they had lain from Sunday until Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you recognise that scene that's shown in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is in the meadow where we carried all the bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The bodies were carried down there and laid out; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We -- we laid them out to be put in the graves, and we put numbers on them. We carried them by tractor because it was a long way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Milosevic, have you got any more questions about the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. Well, we have to clarify this photograph, because this photograph was taken as if people had fallen there, not as if they had been brought there. It's not that they look as if you had brought them Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there and placed them there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please have the photograph shown on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is this a photograph of executed persons or of persons who were brought in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He has given his evidence about this. It's a scene which he says he recognises. Just a moment. The bodies were brought there, and he's described that, and put in the meadow. Now, we've had evidence about this photograph, Mr. Ryneveld, as I recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, Liri Loshi is on our witness list, would have given evidence but will be coming later on, the one who took --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But it's been produced, hasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, we do have this. But I did want to indicate that the witness has testified that he can't see. That is what I understood his evidence to be. Your Honour may have got the impression from the witness that he recognised the scene in this photograph as being a location where they took bodies. That is not what I understood. I might deal with that on re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can deal with it in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, your time is now up. Mr. Tapuskovic, have you any questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I haven't finished even with the photograph, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've had -- you have had your 45 minutes. It's a matter for you how you spend it, and you've wasted much time with this witness anyway. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I would just like to clarify something with this witness. Page 5, paragraph 4, the last sentence of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Draga, a short while ago, you said that you did not know whether Sadik Xhemajli was a commander of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was commander or not. What I mean is that he took part in the funeral.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But in your statement that we are dealing with today and that you gave on the 11th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, could you hand the photograph back, because we'll just get it clarified with counsel at the end. Could you hand the photograph back. We'll get it clarified and then you can get it back. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is their photograph, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, but it's your copy. Yes. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In your written statement, Mr. Draga, you said the following: "This detailed list of 144 bodies was made by Sadik Xhemajli who was local KLA commander." That's what you said when you first gave your statement and that differs from what you said here today. How do you explain this?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: That's what I said before, and that's what I say now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So he was the local commander of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was commander or not. What I'm saying is he was the main organiser in the funeral on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It says something completely different here, but if that's what you're saying, I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can read that. Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Very briefly. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Witness, do I understand you to say that your eyesight is not very good at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When you looked at the photograph -- perhaps you could just take that photograph in your hand, if you would, please. See the photograph to the left there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I can -- I can pick up the photograph, and I can see that it's -- I can't really see it very well, but I believe it's that meadow where the bodies are. Here was the meadow, the graves were over here in a row, and the bodies were laid over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Are you able to tell by looking at that photograph whether that is a photograph of the bodies where they were before you picked them up or whether or not it is the location where you and others took the bodies to? Are you able, with your eyesight, to be able to tell us for sure whether you know which of those two scenes it may be?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGA
utterances.text: I can't make it out. It looks more like the place where we took the bodies to, the meadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But you're going to call Mr. Liri who called the --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Liri Loshi is the man who was there, and I will show -- you have already seen his video. The reason Your Honours have had evidence of that, in the opening I showed a very brief clip of this, and I will select no more than a three-minute portion showing the three groups, of which this is one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So effectively we will be returning to this particular photograph and we can have it clarified then by the person who took it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: By the person who took it; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Draga, for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence. It's now concluded. You're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And perhaps I spoke rather hastily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No more than anybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The Prosecution will call Mr. Hani Hoxha. While we're waiting for the witness, his evidence is relevant to two pages in the Kosovo atlas. That would be page 24 and page 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Does the witness have to wear dark glasses for some medical reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I believe he does, Your Honour. These are prescription glasses. His eyesight is not the best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. Take the declaration, if you would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The usher has the declaration. If you would read it out, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And if you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, is your name Hani Hoxha?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Hoxha, were you born on the 16th of May in 1937?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were you born in the city of Gjakove in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Hoxha, on the 22nd of April, 1999, did you give a statement to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor concerning the events that you witnessed and experienced in Kosovo during 1999?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And on the 14th of March of this year, 2002, in Gjakove in Kosovo, did you have an opportunity to review a copy of the statement that you gave in 1999 in the presence of a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor and a presiding officer appointed by the Registrar of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And Mr. Hoxha, on that occasion in March 2002, did you confirm that the copy of the statement that you reviewed was a true and accurate copy of the statement that you provided in April of 1999?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to ask the Trial Chamber's permission to go into private session very briefly to discuss a matter related to a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, Hani Hoxha is a Kosovo Albanian man, a Muslim, who spent 40 years teaching sports and physical education in Kosovo. When the events described in this statement occurred, he was nearly 62 years old. Mr. Hoxha first describes the events that occurred in his neighbourhood of Gjakove in late March 1999, when Serb forces entered the compounds of his neighbours and killed Mr. Shefqet Pruthi and Mr. Avni Ferizi. When the relatives of these victims spoke to the local police about these killings, they were told: "Go and complain to NATO." Following these killings, Mr. Hoxha, his wife, and his daughter Flaka, decided to seek shelter in the compound of Mr. Hoxha's older daughter Tringa and her husband Lulezim Vejsa. For several days and nights, 24 persons - men, women, and children - stayed in the Vejsa compound. During the nights, the 21 women and children would stay in a basement underneath a business operated by Lulezim Vejsa. The three competent adult men present, Hani Hoxha, Lulezim Vejsa, and Behar Haxhiavdija, would keep watch outside in the courtyard of the compound or in the main house. On the fifth night, at about 12.15 a.m., between the 1st and 2nd of April, 1999, Mr. Hoxha was woken up because a vehicle was trying to break through the gate and enter the Vejsa compound. Previously, the men and women present in the compound had agreed that if Serb forces attempted to break in, the men would flee because it was believed that the Serb forces would only harm the Kosovo Albanian men present and would not harm women and children. After he saw eight to ten uniformed men, some wearing masks, enter the compound, Mr. Hoxha fled over several walls and left the compound. However, Mr. Hoxha remained hidden close by and heard gunshots, the sounds of burning homes, and the sounds of voices saying, "Spare me. Don't kill me." After hiding for seven or eight hours, Mr. Hoxha returned to the Vejsa compound. There he found that the basement where he last saw his family members had been burned, as well as the home of his son-in-law, Lulezim Vejsa, which had collapsed to the ground. In another burned home in the same compound, Mr. Hoxha found the burned body of Hysen Gashi, the uncle of Lulezim Vejsa. On that evening, Mr. Hoxha lost his wife, two daughters, and five grandchildren, and a total of 20 persons were killed in the Vejsa family compound. Mr. Hoxha was subsequently told by a survivor that the victims were shot and burned in the house. Mr. Hoxha decided to join a column of Kosovo Albanian persons leaving the city of Gjakove and heading for the border of Albania. This column was about three kilometres long. The column of people passed through the old part of Gjakove, which had been completely burned by this time. At the exit of the town, policemen directed the Albanians to throw away their identification papers. Several kilometres outside of Gjakove, the column was stopped by members of the Yugoslav army. Everyone in the column was forced to sit down for several hours, and then the column continued again. As the column approached the border, Mr. Hoxha saw Yugoslav army soldiers transporting elderly Albanians on tractor trailers towards the border. Closer to the border, Serb police again asked the persons in the column for their identity documents. Mr. Hoxha eventually crossed the border into Albania and made his way to Tirana.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, this is the incident, the murders which are also referred to as being in Milos Gilic Street; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. Absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And in the indictment, I'll be reminded, is there a schedule referring to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There is, Your Honour. I'm afraid to give you the wrong reference number, but there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's on Schedule G. During the adjournment, could you prepare to answer my question regarding the clarification whether Lulezim Vejsa was the son-in-law of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He doesn't appear on the schedule or is that a different name?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Because the son-in-law survived, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now. It's the appropriate time. Mr. Hoxha, could you remember during the adjournment, please, not to speak to anybody about your evidence, although it hasn't really started, until it's over. We're going to adjourn for twenty minutes, so would you be back, please, just after ten to the hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I ask my questions, I would like to draw your attention to one thing. There are two more witnesses to which I wish to draw your attention. Ismet and Behar Haxhiavdija. Their statements are very much linked to the statements of this witness, and there are major discrepancies among them. And I would think it reasonable to hear these witnesses in succession and then it would be much clearer to everyone what had really happened, because Ismet Haxhiavdija says in his statement that Gjakove was shelled almost every night all night, beginning with the 24th of March. According to my information, this specific locality, the Milos Gilic Street, was hit by a NATO bomb. And you have just heard Mr. Saxon, too, saying in his summary that the house was razed to the ground. Therefore, it is indubitable that we could see things much more clearly if we followed the course of action I suggested. And now I can start asking my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there's nothing we can do about that. It's for the Prosecution to arrange to have witnesses here. Those witnesses, as I recollect, were on the list and were, no doubt, sent home during the break which has occurred. Is that right, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's absolutely correct, Your Honour. And the witnesses for this particular crime site were previously scheduled to testify essentially in sequence. However, when the accused became ill, it simply become untenable to keep them here for such a long period of time and we had to rearrange the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not forgetting that the witness whose family was a victim cares to know, to find out why they had suffered and were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the reason for you and your family to seek shelter in the basement of your house?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: The reason was that on the 25th of May, in my neighbourhood, as I said in my declaration, in my statement, there were killings going on. Houses were being burnt down. And that night, my direct neighbour was killed. Another witness told the Court about him, about his death. And then the -- my -- his neighbour, or my indirect neighbour, a very good friend who had studied in Belgrade, was killed. He was executed in the courtyard of his house. And on the next day, the funeral services of Gjakove came and took away the two corpses. And when they did that, there was panic in the neighbourhood. I didn't really know what was going on at the time, because later I realised the night before, in the great market in Gjakove, the great market was burnt down and people had been executed. But that I only discovered later on. The next day, my daughter Flaka insisted that we go to her second sister --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hani, please. Would you answer my questions. Did Serbian forces ever shell or bomb Gjakove?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: You would know that better than I do. What I know is that your forces executed my wife and children and girls. Then they burnt down my house which I built with such -- such -- managed to build with such difficulty over the last years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me why, from when and for how long, was Djakovica without electricity?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Up until 6.00 or 7.00 in the evening, there was no electricity. It was constantly interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that around midnight you saw flames. How come, if you were in the basement?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: I wasn't in the basement at that time. You're mistaken here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How high is the wall which you mention on page 2, the wall which you said you leaned on when you were alarmed by that incident? How tall is that wall?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Probably about a metre and a half or a metre 70. But they were -- it was difficult to get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At what distance from your houses were the houses which were on fire?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: What date are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am talking -- or, rather, we are talking about your description of houses on fire, the houses you observed while leaning on the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The witness, quite rightly, asked the accused what date he was asking him about, because in his statement, the witness describes two different occasions when he was against the wall as homes were being burnt nearby, and I think the accused could clarify what part of the statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it's clear. If I may interrupt, Mr. Saxon. Paragraph 3 -- perhaps the witness could have his statement. In fact, that might help. Let the witness have a copy of his statement. Mr. Hoxha, you are being asked about an occasion, and if you look in the third paragraph of your statement, you say you leaned on a wall, watching the homes of your neighbours burning, you say, which was very close. Can you help us with how far away that was? That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the right of my house was a house which was about ten metres away. Towards the north, there was a house which was 15 or 20 metres. On the other side, there was a house which was three or four metres away from my house; quite nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were all of those houses on fire?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: All -- all the three houses and two cars were on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that at the moment, when you were standing, leaning against the wall and watching the houses burn, a vehicle was trying to break through the gate of the compound, but they failed because the gate was strong. How long did this attempt to break through last? You can see that on page 3 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: At one moment they tried to break through the gate, but it's quite difficult. It's an iron gate that I have. They tried. And I was in the courtyard at the moment. Everyone else was in the basement, my wife and my daughter Flaka and the neighbours whose houses were being burnt at that time. After that attempt, they left and they went to the next house of Shefqet Pruthi, and they got in. Quite awhile went by. They got into the courtyard, and Shefqet Pruthi, with a candle in his hand, went back around the house. They went after him and executed him. They took his daughter, or they took a daughter, brought her out, and they cursed her. One of them said, "We're going to have fun with you tonight, girl." And she said, "Don't touch me. I'm still young. I'm only 15 years old." And one of them struck her, slapped her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hoxha, would you just wait for the next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that after failing to break through your gate, they broke into the house next door. Does it mean they broke into a house which was already burning or not?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: No. They -- there was -- there were two houses, a modern one and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. an old one. One belonged to Shefqet Pruthi and his wife and daughter, and the other house was where the grandfather lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. You answered no, and we can move on. What were you doing while they were trying to break through your gate? You said you happened to be in the courtyard. What were you doing there? Did you run to take cover? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: As I said, it was an old house behind the new house, and I had taken shelter there. And at a certain moment, I thought that my house was going to be burnt too. And so I went out to see what would happen and tried to intervene to save my family members who were still inside the house, whereas the neighbouring house was burnt after Shefqet was executed. And then they continued on to the next house in the same manner, and continued executing people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you said they broke into the neighbour's compound. Did you see that vehicle and the people inside it?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: I didn't see anything because there's a high wall in between. But I heard a lot of noise, and I saw the next day that the gates had been forced open. And I heard the noise and the cursing because, according to what Arta said, there were 20 to 30 people. I heard a lot of voices. That moment, I didn't know what was happening because it was night. And on the first night when the market was burnt, there was no information at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And for how long were you away between that moment and the moment when you found out what you said you later learned about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Which moment do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you have just explained that you were not able to see from your courtyard inside the neighbour's courtyard because of the high wall, and at that moment, you didn't know what was going on in there. But as I understand, you found out the next morning. So from that moment when you were on the other side of the wall and the next morning when you found out what had happened, where were you in the meantime, in the interim?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: After the execution of Shefqet Pruthi, I went out from the basement to the yard to see whether my own house was being burned or not so that I could evacuate the members of my family. At the moment when Shefqet and Avni Ferizi and an old woman were executed, at that moment I left my house and I saw that all the members of my neighbour's family had left their house and had joined me. And we discussed with my neighbours what was happening, and at a certain point I told them all to get into my house. And they all went in, and I stayed in the yard, and at that moment I thought, Well, how should we act? I was wondering. Meanwhile, because the phones were still working, Arta Pruthi, whose father had been executed, called my daughter Flaka and told her that her father had been killed. And my daughter left the house, looked through the rooms to find him, and I was in the yard outside, and when dawn came, my daughter came out and told me that Uncle Shefqet had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Please don't interrupt me. At that moment, I went in and woke up my wife and we went out to Shefqet's wife, and at that moment, I thought that the deceased was in the room but he was still out in the yard. And I asked the lady, "Why is Shefqet not here? Perhaps you should tell the police." And then Shefqet Pruthi, there was his uncle, Hasan Pruthi, who has been a witness. I went to inform Hasan --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hoxha, I'm afraid we must stop you. Time is limited, and the accused has only a limited time for his cross-examination. Therefore, he must be able to ask such questions as he wants. Of course you can explain matters if you want, but we'll hear the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I understood you as saying that you had seen your neighbour Mr. Shefqet going out into the courtyard, holding a candle. I will read out to you from page 2 of your statement where you say: "As soon as those people broke into the courtyard, they set your [as interpreted] house on fire." Full stop. "My neighbour, Shefqet Pruthi, went out with a candle in his hand." Why would Shefqet be holding a candle with all the flames blazing all around him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is something for Mr. Shefqet to have answered if he could have done. It's not for this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only wish to understand his description of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This man is going out, holding a candle, jumping across the wall, with attackers running in pursuit. Have I understood this correctly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Hoxha, can you help us about this? Was this something you saw or something you were told, that he was being pursued by the attackers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that I saw Shefqet with a candle in his hand. This was told to me by his daughter Arta. Perhaps it's not properly translated in my statement, but I said in my statement that I didn't see him but I said that Arta saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We've cleared this up. How many people were there in the courtyard? You didn't see this either. Somebody else told you about it; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: I didn't see a number of people. I heard noises. I heard shouting. Whereas Shefqet's daughter Arta said that there had been 20 or 30 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. Now I understand, because I couldn't understand it from your statement. Does that also mean that his daughter and wife climbed upstairs to the second floor, as you say in your statement? It's something they told you. You couldn't have seen it with your own eyes, could you?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: All these things are what Arta Pruthi said, and I've got nothing to say on my own account about these matters. She is alive and his wife is alive; you can ask them yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You said Shefqet's daughter called your daughter on the telephone around 3.00. That's what I understood you as saying a moment ago. What were you doing between midnight, when you came out, until 3.00?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Staying in the yard of my house, because I couldn't sleep and I was frightened they could come back again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did Shefqet's daughter tell you that she got out of the house or did you see her get out of the house?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: I said that they got her by the hand and threw her out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know how they -- how she managed to find out that the attackers had killed her father? Did she see that herself?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: She did, and his wife did too. The execution took place at a distance of -- at a range of two or three metres. And this needs no comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you manage to see whether the attackers wore any uniforms or, rather, if so, what kind of uniforms they had and whether they had any uniforms at all? Did you manage to identify, at least in the roughest possible terms, these attackers?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: You say that you don't have much time, but I didn't -- I didn't say -- I said I didn't see these people myself, that this is the account of Arta Pruthi.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In connection with Avni Ferizi, did you see that? All of this with Pruthi, you did not see. This belongs to his daughter's statement. Avni and the vehicle breaking in through his door, did you see that yourself? This is in paragraph 5 of page 2 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: I saw the body of my closest friend. And about how it happened, it was his wife Vjollca who told me how it happened. I didn't myself see the execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Even this event that you explain that has to do with Avni, you didn't see that either. When did she describe this to you?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: On the next day. I stayed in the yard of Avni Ferizi and in Shefqet's yard, going from one to the other. I was always on the move until the police came. And then I stayed there until the hearse came and they took Avni and Shefqet away, and escorted only by Shefqet's sister because it was great danger to go to the cemetery. So that is how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since you didn't see any of that, now I'm putting the following question to you: Could you hear them? Because you say that you were in the yard and they were a few metres away from you.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: I heard the noise in my neighbour's yard. I heard cursing in Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But did you hear the gunshots? And generally speaking, all of that.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I heard shooting. I heard shouting. And of course you could hear the shooting even better.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If all of -- if all of it happened the way you put it in your statement, how is it possible, then, that you did not decide to leave from there?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: I left the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how long did you stay at the place where you went to?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Until the 1st or 2nd of April when the other massacre took place on this street.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Before we get to this 2nd of April, after this first event, what did the families tell you, these families that had provided information to you? Why hadn't they fled from town? You even say that their wives had avoided being killed, went to the police, asked for an investigation in no unequivocal terms, spoke to lawyers, et cetera. Can you explain all of that?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: When we went to the police, the police said, "Go and complain to NATO," as if NATO had killed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there perhaps truth in that, that this was a consequence of the bombing?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: That's absolutely ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, then, why were the bodies of the persons killed not buried by the family? Why is it the Municipal Assembly people who came on the next day in a vehicle to bury them? That is on the next page.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: You must ask the two widowed ladies about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that the funeral was carried out in the absence of the family. Did somebody forbid the family and relatives to attend the funeral? Or let me put the question more specifically: Did the police ban the family from the funeral?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: In the yard where the bodies were put in the coffins, the undertaker and the driver and Shefqet Pruthi's sister got into the car because no other room in the car to take them to the cemetery, but the other members of the family were there, present in the yard. But for the rest, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. They did not go to the funeral because there was no room in the vehicle or because they were afraid of someone, as you had put it a short while ago? What is it they said to you?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: The reason is the second one that you gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I understood this to mean the following: You decided to run away, but where? To Lulezim's house which was 500 metres away. Why there?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: On that day when Shefqet and Avni were buried, my neighbourhood was emptied of people entirely. Everybody went away. I stayed with my wife, with my daughter Flaka, and the daughter of the deceased until 5.00 or 6.00 in the evening.
