And at the insistence of my daughter, we went to my other daughter's, Tringa, because we were very scared. And I saw my closest friend, who had always called me "Uncle," killed. I saw these houses burned, and you can imagine the state of this 15 or 16-year-old girl, how she felt in these terrible scenes. So at her insistence, we decided to go to my second daughter's, Tringa, and at that moment she was very much relieved that we went to her because she was rather relieved to see her sister and father.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned in your statement that during the day -- that is to say this atrocity was committed during the night, and then you said in your statement that during the day, life in Djakovica was as normal. I'm going to remind you. This is page 3, paragraph 3, when you say: "We decided to go to Lulezim's house, to my son-in-law's house, Lulezim Vejsa, and my daughter Tringa Vejsa, we did not see anyone on the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. roads and streets except army and police and their vehicles, who did not talk or do anything to us. Luli ran a bar with pool tables and, underneath that shop, was a basement. In there, about 24 or 25 people spent the night in there. The next day, all people went back to Luli's home, which is part of the same compound. Life was almost normal during the day although there was some fear." What do you mean by that, "life was almost normal during the day" in Djakovica after these events?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: I didn't go out in the town, and I didn't see what was happening there. And on the date when I went to my daughter Tringa, I stayed there until the 2nd of April, and I didn't leave the house for a single moment. I didn't see what was happening in the town at all. Perhaps it's wrongly translated, because there can be no question of normal life when people are living in cellars without any chance of going out to buy food or anything of that kind. There was no kind of normal life in Gjakove in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's not what you said. What you say is: "Life was almost normal during the day, although there was some fear." Full stop. That's the entire sentence. "Life was almost normal during the day, although there was some fear." That is the whole sentence. But let us go on. Did NATO bomb Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not hear the interpretation. Let me just have a look at the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you say no. And were you afraid that Djakovica might be bombed?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you afraid of bombing? All of Kosovo, all of Yugoslavia was bombed, and Kosovo the most.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: You mean the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Never. We had a party when NATO intervened because we thought that they would help us and save us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were not afraid that somebody might get hurt or killed in the bombing?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: We weren't afraid because we were certain that NATO wasn't going to kill people but was going to rescue people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If you yourself say that people sought shelter in basements, is seeking shelter in basements a good way of seeking shelter from the army, the police, people who are on foot? What's the difference then between seeking shelter in basements and seeking shelter in other parts of houses if a person is not seeking shelter from bombing?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: It was a reflex response, and in the ordinary house of my brother, there was not room for all these people and so we inevitably had to go to a cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understood your statement to say that around midnight again some attackers barged into the yard of the house that you were in and they opened fire from their automatic rifles. Who were they shooting at? This is page 4, paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: These people, when they got into the yard, the first thing they did was to fire on the main door of the house where I was sheltering during that night. And they woke me from my sleep. I had nodded off, although I was dressed in jacket and trainers. And my wife and all the women who were there said that if anything happened, we should have -- we should go, we men. And that was the procedure, because we thought that they would never do anything to the women. And I still cannot conceive how somebody can kill a child of two or an elderly woman. And I think that the only thing that could be done would be to ask for a public apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, nobody can imagine that, and this is how most people do become victims in the war. Tell me, did you see the attacker then? Who were they shooting at? How many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: When they first came into the yard, I could see that there were about eight, ten. No doubt other people -- others came in, but at that point I was on -- I was fleeing, and I was very ashamed of running away because only ten metres away there was my wife and daughter and other members of my family. And still today I feel ashamed that I have survived and they, my wife and daughter, did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that the attackers -- that's what you say, that the attackers may have been members of the local police which had otherwise harassed the local Albanian population. Does that mean that you were not sure who the attackers were?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: I didn't know the assailants, but there was another document in existence which -- which was given to me by a human rights activist there who made a statement, who saw these people. And I identified all the perpetrators of this massacre. If you are interested in this, this can be offered in evidence. So a person does exist who saw these people and identified them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So who were the attackers then? If this person had identified them, then I imagine you know who these people were. Were they members of the local police? You say they might have been members of the local police. That's what you say in your statement.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: I made this statement. If the Court sees fit, it can be given to you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How were the attackers dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm -- my eyesight is rather poor and it was also dark, and I was unable really to see these things. So I can't say precisely what kind of uniform they had, but I saw that some had regular police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what is a regular police uniform? The normal blue one that policemen wear in the street; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes, a normal uniform. You know what they look like. This is not an important issue for me. The important thing is that 20 people were executed and were burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's important who did that too. So they did not have any camouflage uniforms. They had regular uniforms, these people did. At least some of them, as you had put it.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: You know better who did this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Hoxha, we fully understand how you feel about this, of course. The event was a terrible one. But as you will appreciate, the Court has to try to determine what happened and who was responsible. So any help that you can give should be given, if you can. Were any of the attackers, as far as you could see - and if you can't, just say so - but if you could see, were any of the attackers in camouflage uniforms or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were. There were, but statements about this do exist from the person who saw them with his own eyes. So that would suffice. It would suffice to call him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. But --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To call and hear the evidence of this person in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know if we're going to hear it or not, and at the moment you're giving evidence, so would you do the best that you can, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that your eyesight is very poor. With this poor eyesight, what did you manage to see out of all the things that you described?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's too general a question for him to be able to answer. Now, if you've got a specific question, you should put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. After these attackers barged in, when you started running away across the walls -- as I can see in your statement, you say that some wooden boards fell around you and constituted some kind of a shelter. This is page 4, paragraph 2. I realise that you did not continue running. You stayed there for eight hours. How did all of this manage to fall on you and how did you manage to stay there for eight hours? Did someone come looking for you?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: No. The boards didn't fall on me. But where I was sheltered, there were two walls. I was between two walls and didn't know how to get out. But at the end of the wall, there was another wall, and I remained there because I couldn't go backwards, because something bad would happen to me if I did. It was very narrow in there. There were a few boards in there. Later, I discovered that a carpenter had been working in that area, and so I stayed there for as long as I mentioned. I don't remember. And then I went back to the house where I'd been the night before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I understand that. This is paragraphs 3 and 4 on page 4. I understood that you returned. So you spent eight hours there and then you returned. And now, tell me, what was the name of the neighbour who walked up to you in the yard? You mention him on page 5, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Babalia is his surname. He's in Canada at the moment. When he saw me in the courtyard, he was surprised, because I was really from another neighbourhood. He asked, "Why are you here? What are you doing here?" And I told him I'd taken shelter. And from that -- from that position, I saw that the house had been destroyed and was razed to the ground. And there I went and found members of my family, and I saw some smoke, but I saw from the house next door, I saw the late Hysen Gashi, whose body was entirely blackened and burned. And at that moment, I thought the worst had happened. This neighbour who joined me, when we went out to the ordinary house where we'd been the previous night, that house had been completely razed to the ground, and this neighbour said to me that he had seen a fragment of human flesh. At that moment, I thought the worst had happened because that's how bad news comes to us. I didn't allow myself to investigate, because I was there. I wanted to have a clear memory of my daughters. I didn't want to see my family burned. And at that moment, they took hold of me and took me to another place three houses away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, your time would normally be up, but on this occasion you can have another ten minutes to put some more questions to the witness. From what you said earlier, it appears that you're going to allege that this killing was due to bombing. If that's right, if that suggestion is one you're going to make, you should put it to the witness so he can have the chance to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, precisely, Mr. May. I do intend to raise this question with the witness on the basis of what he himself said a minute ago. He mentioned two elements; the house was razed to the ground and there were parts of human flesh.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Parts of human flesh and a house razed to the ground. Isn't that a clear indicator that this was done by a bomb, the result of a bomb? Yes or no. Carbonised bodies and a house razed to the ground, isn't that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not at all. The executions were -- took place from a distance of one metre. The daughter of my daughter, Sihane, was very -- a personal who moved around a lot, quickly. And at the moment of the execution of her mother and her sister, she managed to get away. And one of the executors chased her and shot her there where she was. So there was -- there was a living witness who saw all these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the interpretation. One of the executors said -- who was perhaps a better person than the other, said, "That's enough shooting. Stop." And the other people -- the other guy said, "No, we're going to execute them all because these are the people who asked for NATO."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Hoxha, you were there yourself at the time in the neighbourhood. Was there any NATO bombing that night on your neighbourhood, a bomb which could have hit your house or the house that your family were in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. There was no bomb that would destroy Luli's house because my house is next door and it's still intact. There's no way a bomb could destroy a house in that way. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's a question for experts to decide. I'm just asking you for the record. You claim there was no bombing that night in that particular locality where your house is. What exact date are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: We are talking about the night of 1st and 2nd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The night between the 1st and the 2nd of April. Thank you. Where were those police forces and, generally speaking, where was the police while you were searching through the burnt house and moving elsewhere that day? Where were the police?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: What police? There was nobody at that house at the time. And then my neighbour found me, but I didn't see anybody else, because there were 44 other people killed in this neighbourhood on that night besides the 20 that I have been talking about, and there were more than 60 people killed in the neighbourhood on that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. How do you know that so many people were killed that night?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: There are data in the possession of the citizens of Gjakove. I would like all this to be a lie, Your Honour, and to go to prison myself, but it's not a lie. I don't think that there's anybody who could say -- stand and say that my wife has been killed, my daughter has been killed, all these members of my family have been killed. There are the graves. There are documents of the FBI. And I never thought I would be here to say this. And maybe, maybe some of those people have taken refuge in Serbia maybe boast of the numbers they have killed. I used to teach Serbian pupils for a long time. Unfortunately, I believe that there are even former pupils of mine who are on the list of people who perpetrated crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hoxha, was there any NATO bombing in that locality in the days preceding the 1st and 2nd of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the bombing of Gjakove, I didn't see it. And according to what I hear, all I know is that the military barracks was bombed on the way out of the city and also the building of the Secretariat for Internal Affairs in the eastern part of the city. I only know about bombing of these two buildings. I don't know of any other bombs falling on Gjakove. And I believe that the consequences of bombing are quite different, if you look at them, from the consequences of the kind of attack that I've been talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After this, you decided to leave the town. How do you explain that the army of Yugoslavia was so considerate to provide the transport for elderly people to the border, for the people who had decided to leave their homes?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: We walked from Gjakove. It was a column about two or three kilometres long, walking through a burnt, charred city. On the way out from Gjakove at the city limits, the regular police, with the army there, took away our identity cards and our documents. I handed them over. And then we walked to a meadow two or three kilometres away from Gjakove, and there they gathered us. And we weren't even allowed to stand up. We were squatting there. And at that moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Hoxha, we must bring this cross-examination to a close. Mr. Milosevic, two more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You stated that out of the -- from the events you described until the time when you left the town, the Yugoslav army, the police and other authorities never offered you any real assistance. That's what you said. They didn't offer you any real assistance. What kind of assistance did they provide?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: What sort of help? I didn't have any help from anybody. And all those people who were with me didn't get any help from anybody. I only got some help from a peasant woman who gave me two pills, tranquilisers, because all the people who were around me at the time thought I was going to die myself. Because you can imagine the state of my mind at that time because my wife and two daughters had been executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was any assistance offered to people who were miserable, afflicted, who were in a very difficult situation? Was any assistance offered by the Yugoslav army, the police, the Yugoslav authorities, that you could see?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: If we can call it help, I saw two or three tractors that carried people, but I don't think that you can call this help because you know what purpose this was for. It was to secure -- it was for transport, and we should have had human transport, not transport for beasts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Tapuskovic, is there anything you want to ask this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in view of what Mr. Hoxha had gone through, I didn't think I would have any questions, but only with regard to what's on page 2, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hoxha, you said that NATO bombs only fell on military barracks which had already been vacated at the time. Now you mention there was only one barracks. Was there one or several barracks in the vicinity of Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Around Gjakove there is one military barracks, two or three buildings there. There is another military barracks in the centre of town, but there were no soldiers there. There are KFOR soldiers there at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to know about this one in the centre of town. Was it bombed?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: No. They were buildings which were built by the Italians before 1936, and they're still in the same form, the same style they were in. And at the moment, there are once again Italian soldiers in them. So they weren't damaged at all. There was no bombing there, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the police station which was targeted by NATO bombs, is it located between buildings, between houses occupied by people?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: No. The building -- that's the first building at the outskirts of Gjakove, coming from Prizren, and there are no real homes around it. On one side of the -- is the Secretariate for Internal Affairs. I heard that the building -- I only heard that the building had been bombed, because I was in Albania at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Hoxha, I only have one question. You mentioned that more than 60 people were killed in that neighbourhood of Gjakove on the night between the 1st and 2nd of April. Can you recall the name of that neighbourhood, please?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: I wasn't from that neighbourhood. My daughter lived there. But it was called Milos Gilic at the time. I think -- Gilic at any rate, but I think Milos was the first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Hoxha.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Hoxha, thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence. It is concluded, you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, I wanted to comment on the statement that we just admitted. It's a matter that arises in relation to many of the statements that we receive here. They are presented in a manner that suggests that what is written is direct, original evidence, when in fact it is hearsay evidence. Now, it is true that in the Tribunal we admit hearsay evidence if it is relevant, but the matter is important for two reasons: Firstly, if in fact it is hearsay evidence and not direct evidence, then we may end up attaching more weight to it than it deserves. It arose in relation to Arta Pruthi and Avni Ferizi. The second way in which it is important is that we may admit the statement in its entirety under 92 bis without cross-examination and then that could be very misleading. There's another way in which it is misleading. It is misleading to the cross-examiner, because when you read on page 1 in English the references to Arta Pruthi and Avni Ferizi, you're led to believe that the witness is testifying to things which he actually saw when that's not the case. And if the cross-examiner is not sufficiently careful to ask the question to elicit the answer that this is something which the witness did not see, then that would be totally overlooked and the cross-examiner would be misled into believing that was original, direct evidence. In my view, it is not the fault of the witness, it is the fault of the person who is taking the evidence, the investigator, and I think you should have your authorities look into this, because we do admit statements in one form or another, and the accuracy of the statements is a matter of great importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: May I respond, Your Honour? Your Honour, the point is certainly well taken. The members of the Office of the Prosecutor do endeavour, as best as they can, to clarify in statements that are drafted on behalf of witnesses when the witness is speaking from personal knowledge and when such a witness is not. We will certainly endeavour, even more strongly in the future, to take extra care in this regard. With respect to the statement of the last witness, Mr. Hoxha, I'd like to respectfully point out to the Chamber that I believe a careful reading of the text, the examples that Your Honour Judge Robinson just gave to me, actually indicates that the witness was speaking from information that he received from another person. The paragraphs that you just referred to me, the witness says: "I found out that my neighbour Shefqet Pruthi was killed then when Shefqet's daughter Arta telephoned my daughter at about 3.00 a.m. in the morning." So there is certainly at least an indication, although I'm certainly in accordance with Your Honour that perhaps it could be indicated more strongly, that this witness received his information on this particular event from someone else. Regarding the killing of Mr. Pruthi, the very bottom of page 2, going on to the top of page 3, the witness says: "I heard the shots at the time but I did not see him killed." So certainly the reader is put on notice that some of the information regarding these events the witness did not see firsthand. Having said that, we will certainly take -- we will certainly give the strongest consideration to the comments of Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, before we adjourn, there's one other matter. A future witness is K30. I am not sure whether there's an application to have him called under Rule 92 bis. I suspect there is. But in any event, we've looked at that, and we're of the view that he should be called live.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was also the Prosecution's view, so we're not intending to file an application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness will be referring to several places, and they can be found at pages 10 and 11 of the atlas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Gjogaj, can you please state your name for the Court.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: My name is Ali Gjogaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: When were you born, Mr. Gjogaj?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: I was born on the 25th of November, 1963.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And are you of Gypsy origin?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What is your origin?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: I am Ashkalli, Albanian speaking Ashkalli.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And what do you do for a living?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: I am -- work for the city of Prizren. I'm a gravedigger.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Gjogaj, you provided the Office of the Prosecutor two statements, one on 27 February 2000, and another one on the 24th of June, 2000; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And you also, in a meeting that you had with the presiding officer appointed by Registrar, you had an opportunity to review the two statements that you gave before, and you confirm that they are correct and true?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution submits the statements into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Gjogaj, at that meeting you also made an addendum, a short addendum to your statement. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: I don't know what addendum you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: You just -- you complemented it with some more information, one paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can the usher show the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Do you remember signing that, Mr. Gjogaj?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The testimony of the witness is the following: The witness is 38 years old, and in 1999, he was employed by the Hygijena cleaning company as a gravedigger. In the spring, April or May, 1999, police escorted the witness, with about 15 other diggers from the Hygijena company to the village of Pusto Selo, Orahovac municipality. Diggers from other areas joined them en route, also escorted by police. They were directed to assist in the exhumation of the bodies from victims of Pusto Selo and in the reburial of these bodies in different locations, including Zrze and Dushanovo, Prizren. On arrival in the village Pusto Selo, the witness noticed Serb military already present. The police instructed the witness and others to exhume bodies. He estimates that they exhumed about 90 bodies. The witness cannot describe the bodies as they were wrapped in blankets or sheets. The witness, with others, took the bodies in trucks to Pristina where they left them guarded by police. The following day, they returned to unload the bodies into two garages opposite Pristina hospital mortuary. Police ordered the witness to assist in the reburial of the dead. He buried bodies in Zrze cemetery. Others were taken, with other gravediggers, in the direction of Orahovac. Some days later, the witness collected ten bodies from the garage and took them to the graveyard in Dushanovo, Prizren, for burial. The witness also assisted in the burial of three others from the garages into the graveyard in Prizren. All the victims mentioned above were from Pusto Selo. On 24 May 2000, the witness identified a site outside Prizren known as "the fire range" to ICTY investigators, giving the following account: About 20 -- about 8.00 one evening in April 2000, the witness, with others from the Hyginea company, went to the firing range, a site known to him as a military training range. Photos of this site can be found in the Suva Reka binder. I believe it is Exhibit number 166, tab 4. There are several photos of that site. On arrival there, he saw two excavators and three trucks. Police were present and it was dark. He saw men dressed in green uniform dig two holes. He describes one as four metres square. About two metres down, bodies were exposed. The witness assisted in taking the bodies from the ground into the trucks. He describes the victims as men, women, and seven or eight children. He estimates between 80 or 90 bodies were taken from one hole which he describes as four metres deep. The witness describes the vehicle that the bodies were placed in as red/white refrigerated Mercedes, 19/21. He describes seeing police in camouflage uniform digging in the other hole and saw bodies from there being also loaded into a similar truck. The same evening as the witness was working in the firing range, he was ordered to go to a refuse tip on the road to Suva Reka. Using another refrigerated vehicle, he went with other gravediggers and describes seeing some excavator as used in the range. The hole was about two metres square, three deep. At about a metre and a half, he saw more bodies, men and women. The witness assisted in exhuming about 20 bodies. These were placed into the refrigerated truck. That's all, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Exhibit number first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 239 for the original and 239A for the redacted version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are employed as a gravedigger in the Hygijena company in Prizren. What is the year you got a job in that company?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: It was after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did you work before that?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: I worked for the same company. I worked for the Vocar enterprise in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On what job?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Street cleaner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So your occupations included street cleaner and gravedigger, the latter after the war. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you go to school at all?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: No. I'm not educated. I've only got five classes behind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us go briefly through your statement and then I'll have a couple of questions for you. On page 1, you said that with some of the managers in that enterprise, men -- a man called Buda specifically, you went to the village to collect bodies in the spring of 1990 [as interpreted] and that the son of the company manager, Mirko, was one of the policemen who was escorting you. You don't know his last name. You know the son. You know his name is Mirko, but you don't know the name of the manager of your enterprise. Do you know his name?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: He's called Mirko. The director of our enterprise is called Jova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The transcript should reflect that it was in the spring of 1999, not 1990, as recorded. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say on page 3 something about the place where you did the exhumation. You don't know whether it was a cemetery, you don't know whether there was a mosque. You didn't see a mosque or a minaret. Why do you stress that? Did the investigator ask you questions about a cemetery, a mosque, a minaret? Why do you explain that you don't know whether it was happening on a cemetery -- at a cemetery? Why do you say that there was no mosque nearby?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: In the village of Pastaselle where we went, we could first of all not -- first of all, we went there to fetch the bodies, but we went with an excavator but the excavator broke down on the way. And so after a few days later, the same policeman came and spoke to our director there in the office that he had and gave our director the order and gave us a car, and we went to the village of Pusto Selo. And when we went there, to Rahovec, we were received by the Serbs, the police, and the army, and we were also met by some workers from the Rahovec municipality. When we arrived, they gave us the order to get -- take the bodies away as fast as possible. And we took them away as soon as we could and took them to the morgue in Prizren. After a few days --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you something else. I'm asking you why you say that you don't know whether it was at the cemetery and why you say that you don't know whether there was a mosque there.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: I didn't see a mosque. And we were ordered by the Serbian police to take away the bodies as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So it was due to the speed that you didn't see the mosque. Then you also say that you saw wooden signs by all the graves, and you do not -- with numbers, and you did not remember the largest number. Do you remember any one of the numbers?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which number did you remember?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: There were numbers up to 90.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you do remember the largest number after all.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: I saw that number at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. This Mirko who you mention was a policeman. You say that Mirko and other policemen were there. I don't know what they were doing there. Mirko was taking pictures of all the bodies that had been dug up; is that right? That's what you said. Took pictures of all bodies. And then some refugees were putting white stickers with numbers on all the body bags; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: The refugees attached numbers to the bodies. They stuck them on, and they photographed them. The main person was Buda. There was Jova, Mirko, but I didn't know the policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that you took this to the morgue, to Pristina, and it says here on page 4: "The guard at the morgue in Pristina said to us that the Court had asked the police in Prizren to examine the bodies. In Prizren, there was no one to carry out a post-mortem. As far as I know, Dr. Hidajet only examined the wounds on the bodies. He never carried out a post-mortem. He did not examine the bodies from Pusto Selo." That means that these corpses were taken to the morgue, they were photographed by the police, and these bodies were carried in order to have a post-mortem carried out; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: They didn't do these autopsies at the morgue in Prizren, although this word "autopsy" is not very familiar to me. They took them directly to Prishtina where they did this autopsy, and no doubt Dr. Hidajet did it, although I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. You are talking about the photographs that were taken of these dead and about their transport to the morgue and about the court in Prizren asking for a post-mortem to be carried out, et cetera. Then further on, on page 5, you say that three bodies that were entered at the town cemetery in Prizren, that you had also exhumed, were charred. Were these victims of bombings, the charred bodies, I mean? Did you have any idea as to how these people had lost their lives?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: We had no idea. These bodies came from Pastaselle. The graveyards at Pastaselle, they were full of civilian people. They were elderly people, people without any kind of - how can I put it? - without -- without any kind of problems with the police, but they were taken and maltreated and who knows what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute, please. I'm asking you about what you were testifying about. I'm asking you about the carbonised bodies that you had exhumed. I was quoting from your statement. Did you find anything out about that? What was it that killed these people?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: I don't know who killed them. They only sent us there to fetch them. I didn't see who killed them, although it is well-known who killed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, then -- let's not dwell on this any longer. Can you say more specifically the day and month in 1999 when you refer to the spring of 1999, when you say you went to Pristina, to the morgue, and these exhumations and post-mortems and photographs that were taken, et cetera? When was this more specifically?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date because I don't have an education. And I just know that sometimes we worked and sometimes we didn't. We were -- we were people who were compelled to work, and I can't remember dates and times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Actually, that means that at that time, you were not a gravedigger, at that time in the spring of 1999. You were a cleaner at this other company.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: That's right. I was a cleaner. But at that time, even cleaners were forced to do this kind of work. We were forced to do this by the police and the army, and we were like their tools, because the bodies were decomposing and there was a terrible smell, and it was weeks before we could recover from this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, where was this cemetery from which you exhumed 90 bodies and then transferred them to the morgue in Pristina where photographs were taken and then these bodies were taken for post-mortems, et cetera. Where was this?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: The cemetery was the cemetery in the village of Pastasella.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. So that was in Pusto Selo. You say that the school was about 300 metres away from the graveyard; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that this place where you were digging up graves, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. near the centre of the village?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: It was the centre of the village because the school was nearby, and there was a suitable place nearby, a meadow, where they were buried one by one, these bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since this was a village, were there other villagers who attended the exhumations?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: No. There were only us workers, and there were soldiers and policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many graves did you dig up personally?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: I said I myself didn't exhume them. There were workers who exhumed them, and we carried them by trucks. There were some workers over here and some over there, and there were some who were specially to dig up the bodies and bring them to the trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So what was your job, then? You did not drive a truck, did you?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what was your job, then? You were not digging up the graves, you were not driving, so what did you do? Did you carry them in and out or what?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: I carried them. When the workers got them out of the graves, they left them on the meadow, and my colleagues and I took them and carried them up to the trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say, during this operation that you carried out, that you do not remember the number involved. So on the basis of what do you claim that you exhumed 90 bodies?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: When I went after the war with the investigators of the ICTY, I saw 90 holes that had been dug up, but -- so this number has come out now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. So as for the number 90, you do not testify to that from the time when you were carrying these bodies to the morgue, but you are talking about the time when you went with the ICTY investigator to the place to find it, and that's when you counted the holes. This was after the war; right?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: What did you say? I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This number is a number that you established after the war, that is to say, when you went with the ICTY investigator.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, could you explain what the procedure was of putting the bodies into the bags when you took them out. You say that the policemen took pictures of every body with a -- with a photo camera, and then the bodies were put into bags. How did all this take place?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: The workers got out -- got the bodies out, and then they prepared their faces. And then some of the police photographed these unknown, unidentified faces, and other workers put them in bags and we took them to the trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that's where stickers were put with numbers. I assume that those were the numbers of the photographs that were taken. What was on these stickers?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: There weren't numbers on the photographs, but there were numbers on the bodies, assigned to then when they were exhumed. I don't know if you understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not quite, but let us go on. In what condition were these bodies that were being placed into the bags?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: They were in very poor condition. They smelled. I think you can imagine what it's like approaching a decomposed body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were all the bodies in the same condition?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: I wasn't able to see. Perhaps some had limbs that were cut off, but the workers put them in the bags as quickly as possible and took them to the trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in addition to photographs, was any other information collected before the bodies were put into the bags? Were lists made? Were any details recorded except for the photographs that were taken before the bodies were put into the bags?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you also say that you put them into two trucks and transported them to the hospital in Prizren; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After the hospital in Prizren, you took them to the hospital in Pristina; right? Or did these bodies remain behind in the hospital in Prizren?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: I said before. First of all, we brought the bodies from Pastaselle to the morgue in Prizren, and they stayed there several days, and then we took them, in the course of several days, to Prishtina where they had their autopsies done, and we took them to different villages and buried them there. I said this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that when you were transporting them to different villages, that during this post-mortem, these bodies were identified as well, that it was established who these people actually were?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: I don't know. There are others who know very well. We were workers; just exhume them and bring them from the morgue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. You say that you transported them to different villages. When you drove them to different villages, did you hand them over to the members of their families or to who?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: No. There were no relatives there. But some bodies from Pastaselle were -- were sent to Rahovec, some remained behind in Zrze, and some of them remained behind in Dushanovo. And three bodies, finally, were left in the Prizren city cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are those the three that were buried later at the cemetery, the ones you said had been carbonised?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 4, you say that you returned some bodies to Prizren and that you were told to put them at another place so that they would not be confused with the other bodies; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: What did you say? I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said, on page 4, that you returned some of the same bodies to Prizren and that you were told to put them elsewhere so that they would not be confused with yet other bodies. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you return bodies on which a post-mortem had been carried out? Did you return them to the hospital in Pristina, or did you just transport them to the various villages there?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: I said before: When the bodies had their autopsies done in Prishtina, we brought them to the Prizren morgue, and then we distributed them among the villages. We sent them to the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Please. You said that what I quoted to you was not correct, and it says here on page 4, paragraph 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. 6, just two sentences. The second sentence is: "We were told to put them at a place that was different to avoid mixing the bodies." Does that mean that these bodies had already had post-mortems carried out on them so they didn't want them to be confused with the other ones, or what?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: The bodies were totally decomposed, and the three bodies buried in the Prizren cemetery, they were left as the truck brought them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Please. All right. You say in your statement that all the bodies were in bags and that you did not see any clothing or any other belongings. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Two paragraphs later, you say: "All the bodies were in bags. All the -- all the body bags were closed. I never saw any clothes or other belongings of the deceased." I'm just asking you whether that is correct. And it says so in your statement, so I cannot establish what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: What did you say once again, please? I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether it was correct what you wrote in your statement. Did you write this statement? Did you write this statement?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you wrote in your statement: "All the body bags were closed. I never saw any clothes or any other belongings of the deceased." Is that what you wrote? Did you write that?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you do not know what kind of bodies were in these closed bags at all?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: No. I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you open the bags and did you look, or are you saying that the bags were closed and you didn't see anything else?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: I was able, at the Prishtina morgue, when they were preparing the bodies, some bags were torn and I saw the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, all right. Now you've given me an explanation. And on the same page, you mention Dr. Hidajet, and you say: "As far as I know, Dr. Hidajet only examined the wounds." Do you personally know Dr. Hidajet?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: I know Dr. Hidajet as a doctor, but I have no other connection with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And did you attend this examination? Were you present during the examination that he carried out?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Dr. Hidajet did not carry out the autopsy on bodies from Pastaselle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If you were not present during the examination, on the basis of what can you say that an autopsy was not carried out when you were not present there? Because on page 4, you say: "When we arrived at the morgue at the hospital in Pristina, we unloaded the bodies and we were told to go away and come back in a few hours."

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: We unloaded them, and we loaded them up, because there were Serbs at the Prishtina hospital who didn't want to get their hands dirty with decomposed bodies, so we did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You were some kind of a group, a mobilised group, a group that was mobilised in order to carry out that job, as far as I understood. Please, could you explain the following to me: On page 5, paragraph 1, you say: "The bodies were already in a state of decay. I never saw a single face. Even if I had seen them, I would not have been in a position to recognise them because of what I've just said." The question is: How do you know that they were in a state of decay when you say that they were in bags and that the bags were closed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's already said that he saw some when the bags were open in the morgue. So he's answered that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, may I remind you there's another part of his evidence, about the exhumations on the firing range, and you've had 35 or so minutes already, if not more.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope I'm going to get to that as well. I do have these questions for him too. Then I'll have to omit some things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, just give me a brief answer to this question: You say in paragraph 2 on page 5, when speaking about carbonised bodies, about three carbonised bodies, you say that these were elderly people and that they were civilians. Can you explain on the basis of what you drew such a precise conclusion that these were elderly people and that they were civilians when these bodies were carbonised?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: You could see some of the garments and moustache and part of the bone structure which hadn't been charred. Part of a moustache we could see and part of the garments, the clothing, were still visible. And you could see an old person, what an old person looks like from his face.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you drew your conclusions on the basis of the bone structure whether these were elderly people or younger people. Do you have any qualification for that? Because you say that you have completed half of elementary school.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: I didn't understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me move on to my next question, because it's no use putting such questions to you, obviously. On page 5, paragraph 6, you say that two or three days later, you loaded 45 to 65 bodies. Doesn't this difference seem a bit too big for you in respect of such figures, 45 and 65? How many did you load after all? Did you load 45 or 65? Because the difference is all of 20. That's what you refer to in your statement.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: I remember when I gave my statement I said at the beginning that I didn't have school education, and so I couldn't know how many bodies had been loaded on the trucks. The Serb police and army told us to get rid of the bodies as quickly as possible and take them to the morgue in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. However, on page 5, one paragraph before last, you say that the forensic team exhumed these bodies and only 15 graves had been Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. dug up. What happened to the other bodies and graves?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Where do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you say? Sorry? I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: I didn't understand what you were saying. What are you talking about? Where do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I said that on page 5, one paragraph but last, you saw -- you were shown the graves. All the bodies were buried in body bags. You saw that 15 graves had been opened, and you are probably referring to the investigator. You mention 15 graves. Where is this difference between 45 and 65 if only 15 graves had been opened? What you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't follow the question. That presupposes, presumably you're saying, that there was one grave for every body. The evidence, as I understood it, that these were mass graves, but I could be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were those individual graves that you referred to in here or were they graves where several people were buried together? Was every body buried individually?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: There was one grave for each body. The bodies were buried individually.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That means one body per grave, Mr. May, not mass graves, although it seems that this term is more favoured here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Further on on the same page, you say that you did not transfer bodies from the garage to Suva Reka. That's page 6, paragraph 8. And then you say that you did transfer them to Suva Reka. Which is true, that you did or you didn't take them to Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: We didn't send any bodies to Suhareke. We sent them to Rahovec, Zrze, Dushanovo and to Prizren. We didn't send any bodies to Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm reading from paragraph 3 from below, from the bottom, on page 6: "You asked me if I transported any bodies from the garage to Suva Reka. I did not do that, and I do not know that anyone else transported bodies from the garage to Suva Reka." All right. I'll slow down. Next paragraph: "However, me, Shefki, and Xhevdet transported six or seven bodies to a place close to the bus station in Suva Reka." Therefore, would you please answer: Did you or didn't you transfer bodies to Suva Reka? You have it both ways in your statement.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: No. I wasn't at work that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What you wrote here in your statement was actually written by someone else, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: I made the statement, and I said what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 7, paragraph 1, you mention a massacre in Pusto Selo. What kind of massacre is that? Do you know of any massacre in Pusto Selo?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: There wasn't a massacre, but there were 90 graves where -- near where a massacre had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What massacre are you talking about and what do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: I saw people who had been murdered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of what ethnicity were the people whose remains you dug up and who were later sent for autopsies, placed stickers on, et cetera, et cetera, taken photographs of? What ethnicity were they?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know. And the period that you describe in your statement coincided with the NATO aggression; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I said the period that you describe in your statement is the time of the NATO aggression, the time when NATO bombed Yugoslavia and Kosovo, of course, in Yugoslavia. Is that the same time?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: It was when the bombing of Yugoslavia took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I must tell you you've got less than five minutes left if you want to ask some questions about the rest of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, I will. I just want to ask him one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Among the dead that you described, were there any victims of the bombing?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: I didn't see any victims of the bombings. I know that there was NATO bombing, but I didn't see any of the victims, especially when I was at the cemetery. There were Serb attacks. That's what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that you transported victims of NATO bombings to the hospital for identification and autopsies in order to establish their identity and cause of death?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When are you suggesting that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is he who claims that this happened in the spring of 1999. As you know, spring begins in end March and ends in end June. So the NATO bombing lasted the entire spring, and he's talking about spring. I'm only suggesting what he claims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you to clarify it. So what you're putting is that the bodies from Pusto Selo which he assisted in exhuming and taking to Prizren, were victims or may have been victims of the NATO bombing. Is that the suggestion?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am asking him whether he had buried and carried any bodies of victims who were killed by the bombing. That was my question, and you heard it, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't at all clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gjogaj, you say you don't remember the exact date when you helped the exhumation. Is that right? It was just the spring of 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in the addendum which you saw earlier, it says: "This statement refers to an occasion in April or May 1999 when I was directed by police to assist in the exhumation of bodies." How did you remember that it was in April or May? Is it correct? Was it in April or May 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember my -- maybe the end of April. I can sort of remember the month, but I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Please. We have two of your statements. You gave one on the 27th of February and the 1st of March, year 2000. You gave your second statement in June, that means some three months after the first one. In the second statement, you speak of some exhumations from the firing range and their placement in a refrigerator truck. Since this is a major event, how come you didn't mention it as being involved in in your first statement? When did that happen? I heard the other side explaining that it was in April 2000. Was it really in April 2000, as the other side put it, or was it at a different time?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes. It's true. Maybe there is a mistake. I said the same thing at the time, but there might have been a mistake. The firing range was later. But it could have been a bit earlier than I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now I'm asking you about this second statement. All these things that you mention in your second statement, which is completely new compared to the first statement of 27 February and March 1, 2000, given in Prizren, why didn't you mention any of these things in your first statement? Why is it that you remember and mention these things only in the statement dated 24th June 2000, the refrigerator truck and the firing range? When did that event occur?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: I think I told you from the start I don't really remember dates. They sent us to work there in the night, in the middle of the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. Could you tell me, were you working as a gravedigger already when you did this job that you mention in your second statement? Were you by that time already employed as a gravedigger?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: No. They -- I was working for the town, but they told four workers who were employed by the town to do this job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Tell me now, when did that happen? I'm not asking you about whether it was daytime or night-time. What month was it?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: It could have been April. Middle of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So when you were going to Pusto Selo, Prizren, Pristina, and all these things that you mention in your first statement, you remembered them well, and you omitted only that one thing which you remembered later and described in your second statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I need to understand this. The statements which I have -- and perhaps, Ms. Romano, you could help us about this. The statements that I have from the witness are dated February or March 2000. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And the first one I have -- the next one I have is June.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: June, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: That is correct. The first one is 27th February and the second one is 24th June, both --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So I don't understand the accused's point. What point is he making?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The Prosecution doesn't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you can ask two more questions. You've had the best part of an hour with this witness, which is beyond your usual time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us clear up one thing. Ms. Romano, in her introductory statements regarding the events described in the second statement, said that they happened in April 2000. Maybe she will now say that it was a slip of the tongue, but that's what she said, and you can check it in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He describes what happened --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Describing events in a statement of June 2000, describing events which occurred in April and May 2000. This is why I say I don't understand the point that you're making.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is why I'm saying that in April 2000, Mr. May, there were no Serb authorities or Serb police in Kosovo. Starting with June 1999, there are no Serb authorities or Serb police in Kosovo. That's the point I'm making, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. What's being put is that there were no Serb policemen in Kosovo at this time. Mr. Gjogaj, can you help about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The police and the Serb army were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid I'm not understanding right now. The events are in 1999, in April 1999. The witness is testifying about events in April and May 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: On the firing range.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The events then are 2000, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Just in the firing range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: But the first ones are in April and May 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are dealing with two sets of events. One at Pusto Selo in 1999 in the spring, the next a year later on the firing range. Now, if I'm wrong about that, I can be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, you're correct. But he's mentioning police went in which event. That's why I don't understand what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I imagine in 2000. Now, Mr. Milosevic, you've got two more questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have we cleared up when this other event occurred, in 2000 or in 1999?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's told you 2000. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was written in my declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. If what he is claiming -- if what he is claiming went on or happened in the year 2000, in April 2000, then I'm not interested in it at all, because in 2000, there were no Serb authorities there at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We've heard your point and we've heard his evidence on it. Now, Mr. Tapuskovic, very quickly, please, if you have any questions, because you've got six minutes left. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll really try very hard, but there are three major discrepancies between the two statements, three very important points. Page 3, second paragraph from the top in the first statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gjogaj, you've said that what has already been read out to you, that you were not able to see what the bodies looked like when they were dug up. That's page 3, paragraph 2 from the top in the English version, and page 4 in the English version, you say: "When the bodies were put back in the bags, all the bags were closed. I never saw any clothes on the bodies." That's what you said in the first statement; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, that point has already been made by the accused and to go over it again isn't going to assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know, Your Honour, but it will. Would you please compare it, Your Honours, with the second statement, page 3, paragraph 6. "All the bodies were dressed in civilian clothes." How does the witness explain this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is he dealing with the same incident? There are two statements, and it may well be he's dealing with different incidents. Yes, Ms. Romano.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I have to point out that there was a mistake in the summary given. That is what is creating, probably, the confusion. On May 2000, he visit the site with investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor, but the events happened in April 1999. That's why I was referring. All the events happened in 1999, the first one and the second one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, page 5, paragraph 4 of the English version, it says verbatim: "You ask me whether I had seen a burnt village or young people among the deceased." And he answers: "The ones I saw were elderly people." That's what he said in the first statement. And in the second one, he says that he had seen seven or eight children. How does he explain that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The children were at the firing range where we dug out the bodies. But in Pastaselle, there were no children. That was -- the children were at the firing range in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my third point, Your Honours: In his first statement, he says that those bodies that had been dug up were put back and reburied. And now in his new statement, he mentions refrigerator trucks. Can he explain whether all those bodies that had been dug up and reburied are the same bodies he's referring to in the second statement? Because in his first statement, he said that all the bodies that had been dug up had been placed back in the same graves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you help us to that, Mr. Gjogaj?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Not in the same graves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you deal with it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The bodies for each person were placed in bags. They were in bags, in body bags.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were they reburied, put back in the graves?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we're going to have to deal with this tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no point trying to go on. There's a muddle about these statements. Mr. Gjogaj, would you come back, please, tomorrow, when we will get this straightened out. Yes. We will adjourn now. 9.00 tomorrow morning. Mr. Gjogaj, could you remember not to speak to anybody about your evidence during this adjournment. Mr. Milosevic, we'll deal with it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I have one remark that cannot wait. Just one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One question that I want to clear up. Please, Mr. Gjogaj, the event involving the exhumation on the firing range, that happened in the year 2000; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What event?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The one he describes in his second statement, the exhumation at the firing range and the refrigerator trucks. That happened in year 2000, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What we're going to do is this: We're going to adjourn now. Mr. Gjogaj, there is no need to go into it. We cannot possibly go on in this way. Clearly there must be clarification and the Court needs to clarify what's happened. The continual references to the first or the second statement --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This clarifies a lot, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't interrupt. We'll go on tomorrow. It is, Ms. Romano, a problem of having these statements, these statements which are not clear, and it leads to confusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I tend to agree with you, Your Honour, and the only thing the Prosecution can say is that, in an attempt to clarify the matter, that's why we created the second statement, and sometimes a third statement. It's our attempt also to clarify the matter as best as we can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely why it's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I am asked to remind you, and I do, Mr. Milosevic, that you will get a chance to re-examine or cross-examine further, a short chance, in the light of this confusion. Yes. Tomorrow morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
